item.title: Is China Misreading the Moment?
item.description: When U.S. President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing. The trade war of 2025 is in abeyance, the two governments have announced a relationship of “constructive strategic stability,” and, to the alarm of American allies, Trump and Xi are planning to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. item.title: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching
item.description:
Purpose

CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution.

Actions to take

CISA urges organizations to take the following actions:

  • Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories.
  • Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems.
    • If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access.
  • Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions.
  •  Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes.

CISA urges network defenders to review the following resource and apply necessary updates:

item.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
item.description:
CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. 

  • CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. 

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. 

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. 

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

item.title: oPt: One Year On, Gaza’s ‘Peace Plan’ Has Failed, Delivering More Death, Displacement, Despair – Humanitarian Scorecard
item.description:
Countries: occupied Palestinian territory, Guatemala, Israel
Source: Islamic Relief

One Year On, Gaza’s ‘Peace Plan’ Has Failed, Delivering More Death, Displacement, Despair – Humanitarian Scorecard

November, 19, 2026

Access the Scorecard

WASHINGTON— One year after an internationally backed ‘peace’ plan for Gaza was launched, it has received a failing score in a scorecard by five leading humanitarian organizations.

The scorecard, led by the Danish Refugee Council, Norwegian Refugee Council, Oxfam, Refugees International, and Save the Children, gave a score of 4 out of 26 to the Trump administration’s 20-point plan that was endorsed by the UN Security Council. This is down from a score of 5 in a scorecard on the same metrics at the six-month mark in April 2026.

The scorecard assesses progress against the 20-point plan’s own objectives related to civilian protection, humanitarian access, reconstruction and economic development, and freedom of movement and return.

Between the ceasefire declaration in October 2025 and mid-November 2026, at least 1,650 Palestinians were killed and 5,975 wounded, more than double the death toll at the six-month mark. Israeli forces now control up to 70% of Gaza, up from 58% at the start of the ceasefire. The UN has reported near-daily Israeli airstrikes in densely populated areas over the past year.

The ceasefire, which was endorsed by UN Security Council Resolution 2803 on 17 November 2025, stipulates an agreed-to minimum of 600 UN-coordinated aid trucks entering Gaza daily. In September, an average of 49 UN-coordinated aid trucks entered Gaza each day with only 2% carrying medical supplies.

Critical shortages of basic medicines and supplies have resulted in deaths from treatable injuries and illnesses. The scorecard, as it did in April 2026, grades humanitarian access in the ceasefire deal with a score of zero.

The Government of Israel continues to obstruct the delivery of shelter materials, medical equipment, and supplies needed to restore water and sanitation services, while nearly the entire population of 2.1 million civilians is struggling to access clean water, healthcare, and adequate food.

All six wastewater treatment plants in Gaza remain out of service and not a single hospital is fully operational.

As Gaza faces its fourth winter with little protection from cold and rain, nearly 1 million Palestinians live in sites at medium or high risk of flooding and 89% of households report rodents inside their shelters.

Already this month a rainstorm flooded more than 70,000 tents and a 9-month-old child was reported to have died of hypothermia.

The organizations urge the UN Security Council, the Board of Peace, and Member States to use their leverage to secure immediate humanitarian access and enforce the ceasefire.

Key recommendations include:

  • Lifesaving Aid and Medical Care: Press Israeli authorities to open all crossings, admit essential supplies, lift restrictions on aid operations, and restore medical evacuations and freedom of movement, including the right to return.
  • Aid Oversight: Member States, working with the Board of Peace, should replace Israeli approval and inspection processes with independent, transparent aid verification.
  • Ceasefire Enforcement and Accountability: Member States should establish UN-mandated monitoring and quarterly humanitarian reporting, and use diplomatic, legal, and economic measures to secure compliance with the ceasefire and UNSCR 2803.
  • Recovery and Reconstruction: Member States and the Board of Peace should ensure recovery protects Palestinians’ freedom of movement, prevents forced displacement, and advances commitments under the New York Declaration.

“One year into the so-called ceasefire, Palestinians are still waiting for the safety and humanitarian relief they were promised,” said Jeremy Konyndyk, President of Refugees International. “People are still being killed, Israeli forces are expanding control of Gaza, and families are facing another winter in flooded tents while desperately needed supplies sit just across the border. None of this is inevitable. Israel has clear obligations both under Trump’s peace plan and under international law to protect civilians and allow humanitarian aid into Gaza. The United States and other UN Security Council members must use their leverage to ensure those obligations are met. The commitments made a year ago mean little if they do not change the reality on the ground.”

“The suffering of Gaza’s 2.1 million people is not inevitable. The world must stop accepting it,” said Jan Egeland, CEO of Norwegian Refugee Council. “Palestinians should have the opportunity to recover, rebuild their lives and work towards a better future. But this is not possible unless Israel fulfils its obligations under international law: opening all crossings, allowing humanitarian aid to enter, and ending its unlawful occupation of Palestinian land.”

“One year ago, the world was promised that Gaza’s children would finally see safety, relief and a chance to rebuild their lives. Instead, they are colder, hungrier, more traumatized and more at risk than they were before. This was supposed to be a roadmap out of catastrophe. Instead, catastrophe has deepened. The international community cannot continue to look away. The children of Gaza do not deserve this,” said Inger Ashing, CEO of Save the Children International.

“Regretfully, the Board of Peace failed the international community and continue to ‎provide political cover for ongoing genocide and atrocities. We call on member states ‎‎— especially those with leverage over Israel – to stop issuing plans and take concrete ‎actions: impose an arms embargo, ensure unconditional humanitarian access, and ‎pursue accountability for war crimes. Protecting Palestinian lives and dignity is not ‎only for Palestinians – it is the last line of defense for what remains of our shared ‎humanity and human values,” said Mohsen Abu Ramadan, Board Member of Palestinian NGOs Network.

“The ceasefire in Gaza is failing and Palestinians are still dying, which is a direct result of policy choices made in Israel, the US, and at the UN. Instead of abiding by the ceasefire plan, the Israeli government is continuing its attacks, forcing Palestinians to try and survive without adequate food, water, shelter, or sanitation, amid open sewage and freezing rain – all while the United States does little to stop it. As we have been saying, the government of Israel must allow aid to enter, end its attacks and collective punishment on all Palestinians in Gaza, and allow the long process of rebuilding to begin,” said Abby Maxman, Oxfam America President & CEO.

“A year into the ceasefire, Palestinians in Gaza are being confined as the Yellow Line expands. Israeli forces now control nearly 70 percent of Gaza, and 1.8 million people are squeezed into displacement sites lacking clean water and sanitation. Families that have already fled up to a dozen times are forced to move again when gunfire and explosions erupt, often with no warning. This is displacement by design, and a ceasefire that allows it is a ceasefire in name only. The international community must use its leverage to halt the expansion of the Yellow Line and guarantee Palestinians’ right to return safely to their homes,” said Lilu Thapa, Danish Refugee Council Executive Director Middle East, Asia and Europe.

This plan by WHH Anticipatory Humanitarian Action Facility (WAHAFA) partners Christian Blind Mission (CBM) and the Presbyterian Church in Cameroon (PCC) shows how Anticipatory Action supports flood-prone communities in Limbe, Fako Division, Cameroon, to act before severe riverine flooding occurs.

This locally developed Anticipatory Action Plan (AAP) combines rainfall forecasts and community observations to trigger early actions addressing health risks, property damage, displacement and food insecurity. Developed with communities, local authorities and organizations of persons with disabilities, the AAP includes drainage clearance, early warning communication and the distribution of water purification tablets, hygiene supplies, mosquito nets and food items.

Using a two-phase trigger mechanism based on forecasts from the National Observatory on Climate Change (ONACC) and local observations of soil saturation, the AAP enables the activation of anticipatory actions with a lead time of approximately 3-9 days and the release of pre-agreed finance from the WAHAFA Fuel funding.

item.title: Madagascar: Southern Africa: El Niño Status and Humanitarian Impacts (October 2026)
item.description:
Countries: Madagascar, Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached Infographic.

OVERVIEW

El Niño conditions are underway and are forecasted to strengthen through late 2026, coinciding with a strong positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD).

Key Messages
I. A high-confidence dry season is forecasted for central and southern parts of Southern Africa. Seasonal forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of below-normal rainfall, prolonged dry spells and above-normal temperatures, while above-normal rainfall and flooding risks are expected in parts of the northern areas of the region.

II. The region remains highly vulnerable following the severe 2023/24 El Niño, which affected an estimated 54.4 million people and contributed to widespread food insecurity, livelihood losses and disease outbreaks. Currently, humanitarian needs remain elevated, with 11 million acutely food insecure people across the region, while funding levels remain low.

III. Southern Africa experienced one of its largest cholera outbreaks during 2024-25, increasing public health concerns entering the 2026/27 El Niño season.

IV. Governments and partners are advancing contingency planning, preparedness and anticipatory action measures to reduce the expected impacts on food security, water resources, livelihoods, health and protection during the 2026/27 season.

V. Critical funding gaps in preparedness and anticipatory action are undermining efforts to protect vulnerable communities from the expected impacts of El Niño.
